name: Murata-grm_GRM1885C1H222JA01
title: GRM1885C1H222JA01: 2200 pF, 50 V DC, C0G multilayer ceramic chip capacitor, 1608M (0603)
summary: A surface-mount multilayer ceramic chip capacitor of 2200 pF ±5 %, rated 50 V DC, in the 1.6 × 0.8 × 0.8 mm (metric 1608, EIA 0603) body. Its temperature characteristic is 5C, C0G in EIA terms, with a coefficient of 0 ±30 ppm/°C, and it works from -55 °C to 125 °C. It is offered for consumer, industrial, non-implant medical (GHTF class A/B/C) and automotive infotainment equipment, and may be flow or reflow soldered. The four orderable numbers differ only in reel size and tape pitch.

notes: The number reads, field by field: GRM series; 18 for the 1.6 × 0.8 mm footprint (L × W); 8 for the 0.8 mm thickness (T); 5C temperature characteristic; 1H rated voltage, 50 V DC; 222 capacitance, 22 × 10² pF = 2200 pF; J tolerance, ±5 %; A01 Murata's individual control code; then the one-letter package code.
W8P4 is 8 mm wide tape with a 4 mm cavity pitch; W8P2 has a 2 mm pitch.

operation.text: The 50 V DC rating is the most that may sit across the terminals at any instant. With AC riding on DC the zero-to-peak value must stay under the rating; for pure AC or pulses the peak-to-peak value must. Surges, static discharge and pulse spikes count against the same limit. Overvoltage can break down the dielectric layers and short the capacitor, after a time that depends on the voltage and the ambient temperature.

AC or pulse current through the capacitor heats it through dielectric loss, most at high frequency. The body surface, self-heating included, must stay within the 125 °C maximum operating temperature. For parts rated under 100 V DC, the load is limited so the body rises less than 20 °C above a 25 °C ambient.

The 5C (C0G) characteristic has a 0 ±30 ppm/°C temperature coefficient between 25 °C and 125 °C, with the cold-side capacitance changes of Table A. Capacitance ageing and the DC and AC voltage dependence of capacitance are stated for high dielectric constant types.

General-purpose Murata MLCCs are designed for equipment with a life of about 10 years, and reach more than 10 years at 80 % of rated voltage or less with the product temperature at least 20 °C below its maximum operating temperature. Consumer-specific types are designed for over 5 years under the same conditions. Estimated useful life is the time to a 1 % cumulative failure rate in continuous use; the curves are estimates, not a guarantee.

Board flexing cracks chips. Lay the chip with its long axis across the direction in which the board bends. Near a separation line, turn the chip parallel to the line, cut slits in the line and keep the chip back from it; do all three where possible. Keep chips away from screw holes, where tightening bends the board.

Set the lowest point of the placement nozzle so it does not bend the board, and support the board from below. Dirty nozzles and worn locating claws load the chip unevenly and crack it; clean, check and replace them on a schedule.

Preheat both chip and board so the step from the preheat to the solder temperature, ΔT, stays within 190 °C for this size; keep the same limit between the part and any solvent it is dipped in after mounting. Peak at 240 to 260 °C in air or nitrogen with Sn-3.0Ag-0.5Cu. A peak below the peak the solder supplier recommends can bring poor wetting, voids, whiskers, weak joints, poor self-alignment, tombstoning or shifting. Too much paste makes a tall fillet that passes board stress into the chip; too little leaves a weak joint. Repeated passes add up and must stay within the allowable time-temperature curve.

The 18 size may be flow soldered, with ΔT within 150 °C, preheat peak 100 to 120 °C and solder peak 250 to 260 °C. Too long or too hot a dip leaches the terminations, weakening adhesion or losing capacitance where inner electrodes part from the termination. The fillet should stay below the top of the chip. Halide in the flux should be 0.1 % max., and leaching should not exceed 25 % of the chip end edge, nor 25 % of the land-side edge when mounted.

Chips glued down before flow soldering are usually fixed with epoxy. The adhesive should hold the chip through placement and soldering, keep its strength when wet, dispense and hold shape well, have a long pot life and short cure, not corrode the chip or board, insulate well, give off no toxic gas and carry no halogen compounds. Too little glue or too short a cure lets the chip shift or fall off; too much spreads onto the lands and spoils the joint; too hot or long a cure weakens the bond and oxidises the terminations. The glue dot sits between the lands under the chip body, on resist.

Preheat chip and board before touching up with an iron: tip 350 °C max., preheat 150 °C min., ΔT within 190 °C, and let the board cool slowly. Work quickly with a tip of ø3 mm or smaller and ø0.5 mm or thinner wire, without touching the chip with the iron. A spot heater, which warms chip and board together and gives less thermal shock, is held 5 mm or more away at 45°, outlet 400 °C max., for under 10 s on chips up to 3.2 × 1.6 mm.

Support the board under test probes, as close to the probe as possible, so probing does not flex it. Avoid ultrasonic cleaning strong enough to resonate the board. Separate panels with a router where possible; hand or nipper breaking stresses the chips most. Hold boards by the edges with both hands, set the nozzle bottom point for back-side placement on the straightened board, support the board when inserting leaded parts or connectors, and use a torque driver on screws. Do not use a dropped board or a dropped capacitor, and do not reuse a capacitor removed from equipment.

Chips are more sensitive than leaded parts to bending and thermal stress, and an oversized fillet multiplies it, so lands are sized to limit fillet height. A board whose expansion differs greatly from the chip, such as a fluorine resin board or a single-layer glass epoxy board, can crack it through thermal cycling. When moving to a smaller chip, revisit trace width, trace direction and copper thickness as well as land size.

Resin shrinkage on curing and a mismatch in expansion can crack the chip or lower its insulation. Choose a low-shrink resin with expansion close to the chip, optionally over a silicone buffer, and a low-moisture-uptake resin such as epoxy. Strongly acidic coatings or fluxes corrode the chip.

Store at +5 to +40 °C and 20 to 70 % RH, preferably below 30 °C, away from corrosive gases (hydrogen sulfide, sulfur dioxide, chlorine, ammonia), direct sunlight and condensation, and use promptly. In service, keep the capacitor away from water, oil, brine, conductive liquids, ozone, UV, radiation, toxic gas and condensation; damp-proof the assembly where condensation can occur. The capacitor is not a safety-certified part; where a shorted capacitor could cause shock, smoke or fire, add a fail-safe such as a fuse.
Sn-Zn based solder lowers MLCC reliability; Murata is to be consulted before using it.
